stories.author: The Lever team
stories.title: 9/11 Changed America — And Built Trump’s Playbook
stories.text: You cannot understand the executive power Donald Trump is wielding today if you do not understand how 9/11 was used to create that power. I have been perseverating on that truth in the lead-up to today’s 25-year anniversary of the terrorist attack that altered so much — including my own life. I remember that day well: I was working on Capitol Hill at my new job working for Democrats on the House Appropriations Committee. As a plane was heading for the Capitol complex, everyone made a mad dash for the exits. In the chaos, I found two familiar faces: my old boss, Bernie Sanders, and his chief of staff, Jeff Weaver. We made our way to a restaurant blocks away from the Capitol, where we learned the grim news that thousands of Americans had been murdered — and sensed that everything was about to change. My job abruptly shifted away from debates over the Bush administration’s spending cuts and tax cuts to all things national security. The work became all about challenging the White House’s master plan to dupe America into the Iraq War and secretly build a massive surveillance apparatus that mimicked the terrifying panopticon depicted in the then-recent film Enemy Of The State . stories.title: Dan Osborn Knows Why Democrats Keep Losing Nebraska
stories.text: LISTEN NOW: Registered Republicans outnumber Democrats almost 2-to-1 in Nebraska, and the few Democrats who hold elected offices in the state are overwhelmingly conservative. But like the rest of the country, Nebraska is feeling the strain of soaring prices, the data center boom, and Trump’s tariffs. Is the state ready for a change? Today on Lever Time , David Sirota visits rural Nebraska to meet Dan Osborn, the former union president and independent who is challenging Sen. Pete Ricketts (R-Neb.), the son of a billionaire, for his seat. In a state where “Democrat” is a dirty word, could Osborn’s populist campaign become a blueprint for breaking free from a dysfunctional two-party system? TAIZ, Yemen*—This week, as Ansarallah forces advanced by the hour to seize the port city of Mokha and secure access to the strategic Bab al-Mandab strait off the coast of Yemen, residents of Taiz braced for more fighting. Over the past week, some of the fiercest battles between Ansarallah (also known as the Houthis) and Saudi-backed Yemeni government forces took place in the hills surrounding Taiz—a crucial trade hub in southwestern Yemen, situated between Ibb, Mokha, Hodeidah, and Aden. On Wednesday, Saudi Arabia bombed five Yemeni governorates more than 50 times in a single 12-hour span. On Sunday, powerful explosions shook Taiz and several residential areas were shelled. The Yemeni government attributed the explosions to Ansarallah. Ansarallah neither claimed the bombings nor denied them, but the fighting proved decisive ahead of Ansarallah’s capture of Mokha later in the week. stories.author: The Lever team
stories.title: The Big Tech Alums Building Trump’s AI War Machine
stories.text: As lawmakers demand Congress put artificial intelligence safeguards in place amid new warnings from AI whistleblowers, the Trump administration is using a new, obscure office to do exactly the opposite. The agency, which is dedicated to turning the U.S. military into an “ AI-first warfighting force ,” is staffed by alumni of Amazon, Palantir, Meta, and Salesforce. All firms that are at the center of the government’s AI contracting boom and which have the most to gain from the minimal implementation of AI safeguards. The Department of Defense founded the little-known Chief Digital and Artificial Intelligence Office (CDAO) in 2022 when it merged multiple offices, including the Joint Artificial Intelligence Center, the Defense Digital Service, and the Chief Data Officer, into a single entity. It now leads all things AI at the Pentagon, from “the development and deployment of algorithmic warfare” and drafting AI-related policy to helping guide the procurement of AI systems from private contractors like Amazon and Palantir. stories.text: This is essential to our mission: to report on what matters most, beholden only to the truth. In that spirit, we made a commitment to ensure that our journalism is free for everyone, not locked behind a paywall. But that means we rely on the voluntary support of our community of readers. A video that recently went viral on Iranian social media shows people eating caviar and rare salmon for breakfast in Tehran, a meal costing around 10 million tomans ($50), the monthly wage for many Iranians. Another viral video shows a man wrapping a thick piece of red meat between two layers of bacon, adding additional meat, and then wrapping the concoction in a bun soaked with fat. Such videos have become increasingly popular in Iran as the country grapples with the rising cost of meat and other food staples. The head of Iran’s Association of Meat and Protein Products Packing Industry said in late May that in response to the high prices, demand for meat products had fallen 50% compared with the previous year. stories.author: Matt Taibbi
stories.title: On Escaping This Horrible Era
stories.text: Racket readers may have noticed it’s quiet in here. There are three reasons, two temporary. I’ve been working on a book for two years and am in a home stretch. The second involves a breaking-type story that is a document-heavy slog, but coming. The third is more complicated. Call it an existential pileup. When I entered journalism I filed as unimportant the fact that many of my heroes left warnings to avoid the profession. The most famous are known, like Hunter Thompson calling his profession a place where “thieves and pimps run free and good men die like dogs,” or Oscar Wilde saying, “journalism is unreadable, and literature is not read.” Balzac said journalism was a “bottomless pit of iniquity and treachery and lies,” while Flaubert, whose Dictionary of Received Ideas was one of a handful of books I lugged around the world throughout my twenties, wrote in a letter to George Sand that the press is a “school of demoralization” that “dispenses with thinking.” H.L.
